summary.text: A finite check establishes a stable run-length pattern from the seventh transformed row, and an inductive preservation argument converts the subsequent row sums and auxiliary lengths into an eight-dimensional positive linear recurrence. Coordinate domination in this recurrence gives submultiplicativity of the shifted row sums, so Fekete’s lemma applied to their logarithms yields convergence of the normalized logarithms; exponentiation and removal of the fixed index shift give the desired root limit.

full_proof.text:
Let \(R(w)\) denote the list of run lengths of a finite list \(w\), and let \(\bar w\) denote reversal. Concatenation of lists will be denoted by juxtaposition (or, when it improves readability, by \(\mathbin{\|}\)). Thus, for example, if
\[
w=(4,4,7,7,7,2),
\]
then \(R(w)=(2,3,1)\).

Let \(T_n\) be the rows defining A381587, so
\[
T_1=(1),\qquad T_2=(1),\qquad T_3=(2),
\]
and, for \(n\geq 3\),
\[
T_{n+1}=R(\bar T_n)\,T_n.
\]
The sequence under consideration is
\[
a(n)=\sum_{t\in T_n}t.
\]
We prove that \(a(n)^{1/n}\) has a limit.

We first collect some elementary facts about run lengths. If two nonempty lists \(p,q\) are concatenated, there are two possibilities at their common boundary. If the last entry of \(p\) and the first entry of \(q\) differ, then
\[
R(pq)=R(p)R(q).
\]
If those two entries agree, the last run of \(p\) and the first run of \(q\) merge, so \(R(pq)\) is obtained from \(R(p)R(q)\) by replacing the last entry of \(R(p)\) and the first entry of \(R(q)\) by their sum. We call this latter operation “gluing” and write it as
\[
G(R(p),R(q)).
\]
These assertions follow immediately by scanning the concatenated list. They include the cases where one of the lists is empty, with the evident convention.

Reversing a list reverses the order of its runs without changing their lengths. Hence
\[
R(\bar w)=\overline{R(w)}.                                      \tag{1}
\]
Every entry of \(R(w)\) is positive, and if \(w\neq\varnothing\), then \(R(w)\neq\varnothing\). Also,
\[
\sum R(w)=|w|                                                   \tag{2}
\]
because the runs partition the entries of \(w\), and
\[
|R(w)|\leq |w|.                                                 \tag{3}
\]

It is useful to reverse the rows. Define lists \(W_k\) by
\[
W_0=(2),\qquad W_{k+1}=S(W_k),\qquad
S(w):=w\,\overline{R(w)}.                                      \tag{4}
\]
We claim that
\[
\bar T_{k+3}=W_k                                                \tag{5}
\]
for every \(k\geq0\). This is true at \(k=0\), since \(T_3=(2)\). If it is true for \(k\), then
\[
\bar T_{k+4}
 =\overline{R(\bar T_{k+3})T_{k+3}}
 =\bar T_{k+3}\,\overline{R(\bar T_{k+3})}
 =W_k\,\overline{R(W_k)}
 =W_{k+1},
\]
which proves (5) by induction.

Consequently,
\[
a(k+3)=\sum W_k,                                                \tag{6}
\]
and, using (2) in the row recursion,
\[
a(k+4)=a(k+3)+|W_k|.                                           \tag{7}
\]
Moreover, directly from (4),
\[
|W_{k+1}|=|W_k|+|R(W_k)|.                                      \tag{8}
\]

The main combinatorial point is that, from a fixed point onward, the lengths \(|R(W_k)|\) and \(|R^2(W_k)|\) also satisfy stable recurrences. We now prove this carefully.

We use the following structural condition on a pair of lists \((x,v)\). Call the pair good if there are lists \(C,D,E,V\) such that:

1. both \(x\) and \(v\) begin with
\[
(2,1,1,1,3)
\]
and both end in \(1\);

2. one has
\[
R(x)=C(1),\qquad R^2(x)=D(6),\qquad R^3(x)=E(1);                \tag{9}
\]

3. the auxiliary lists have the following endpoint forms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&C=(1)C_t=C_i(1),\\
&D=(1,1)D_t=D_i(1),\\
&E=(6,1)E_t=E_i(3);
\end{aligned}                                                   \tag{10}
\]

4. the third iterated run-length list connects \(x\) to \(v\) by
\[
R^3(x)=(6)\,\operatorname{tail}(v);                            \tag{11}
\]

5. finally,
\[
R(v)=V(1),\qquad V=(1,3)V_t.                                   \tag{12}
\]

Here \(C_t,C_i,D_t,D_i,E_t,E_i,V_t\) are arbitrary lists; the notation simply records the stated beginnings and endings.

We next show that goodness is preserved by applying \(S\) to both lists:
\[
(x,v)\text{ good}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(S(x),S(v))\text{ good}. \tag{13}
\]

Assume the conditions above. Two preliminary consequences of (9) and the endpoint data are
\[
R(C)=D(5),\qquad R(D)=E.                                       \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, \(C\) ends in \(1\). Appending the final \(1\) in \(R(x)=C(1)\) therefore lengthens the last run of \(C\) by one. Since
\[
R(C(1))=R^2(x)=D(6),
\]
the run-length list of \(C\) must be \(D(5)\). Next, \(D\) ends in \(1\), while the appended entry in \(D(6)\) is \(6\). These entries differ, so
\[
R(D(6))=R(D)(1).
\]
Comparing this with \(R^3(x)=E(1)\) gives \(R(D)=E\).

We now compute the first three run-length iterates of \(S(x)\). The result is
\[
R(S(x))=C(7)\bar D,                                             \tag{15}
\]
\[
R^2(S(x))=D(5,1)\bar E,                                        \tag{16}
\]
and
\[
R^3(S(x))=(E(1))\,\overline{R(v)}.                             \tag{17}
\]

To verify (15), use \(R(x)=C(1)\), so
\[
S(x)=x\,(1)\bar C.
\]
The last entry of \(x\) is \(1\), and hence the new initial \(1\) merges with its final run. On the run-length level this glues \(C(1)\) to \(R((1)\bar C)\). By (1) and \(R^2(x)=D(6)\),
\[
R((1)\bar C)=(6)\bar D.
\]
Gluing the last entry \(1\) of \(C(1)\) to the first entry \(6\) of \((6)\bar D\) replaces them by \(7\), giving (15).

For (16), first use (14): \(R(C)=D(5)\). The entry \(7\) in (15) differs from the final entry \(1\) of \(C\), and it also differs from the first entry of \(\bar D\), which is \(1\). Thus the run occupied by \(7\) is a singleton. By (1) and \(R(D)=E\), the run lengths of \(\bar D\) are \(\bar E\). Therefore
\[
R(C(7)\bar D)=D(5)(1)\bar E,
\]
which is (16).

For (17), the boundary values in (16), together with the facts that \(D\) ends in \(1\) and \(E\) ends in \(3\), give
\[
R\bigl(D(5,1)\bar E\bigr)=E(1,1)\,\overline{R(E)}.             \tag{18}
\]
On the other hand, since \(E\) ends in \(3\), appending \(1\) does not merge a run, and therefore
\[
R(E(1))=R(E)(1).                                                \tag{19}
\]
By (11), \(E(1)=R^3(x)=(6)\operatorname{tail}(v)\). The list \(v\) begins \((2,1,1,1,3)\). Replacing its first entry \(2\) by \(6\) changes no equality or inequality between adjacent entries, because both \(2\) and \(6\) differ from the following \(1\). Hence
\[
R((6)\operatorname{tail}(v))=R(v).
\]
Together with (19), this says
\[
R(E)(1)=R(v).
\]
Substitution into (18) gives exactly
\[
E(1,1)\overline{R(E)}=(E(1))\overline{R(v)},
\]
which proves (17).

These formulas have all the endpoint forms needed for the new pair. To see this explicitly, write the decompositions from (10) and (12) as
\[
D=(1,1)D_t,
\qquad E=(6,1)E_t,
\qquad V=(1,3)V_t.
\]
Then (15) can be written
\[
R(S(x))=C'(1),
\qquad C':=C(7)\bar D_t(1).
\]
Thus \(C'\) starts with \(1\) and ends with \(1\). Formula (16) becomes
\[
R^2(S(x))=D'(6),
\qquad D':=D(5,1)\bar E_t(1),
\]
so \(D'\) begins with \((1,1)\) and ends with \(1\). Formula (17), using \(R(v)=V(1)\), becomes
\[
R^3(S(x))=E'(1),
\qquad E':=E(1,1)\bar V_t(3).
\]
Thus \(E'\) begins with \((6,1)\) and ends with \(3\).

Also, (17) and (11) imply the required new connection. Indeed,
\[
R^3(S(x))=(E(1))\overline{R(v)}
          =(6)\operatorname{tail}(v)\overline{R(v)}
          =(6)\operatorname{tail}(S(v)).                       \tag{20}
\]
Both \(S(x)\) and \(S(v)\) retain the initial block \((2,1,1,1,3)\). They also end in \(1\): the last entry of \(S(x)\) is the first entry of \(R(x)\), namely the first entry of \(C\), which is \(1\), and similarly the last entry of \(S(v)\) is the first entry of \(V\), also \(1\).

It remains only to check that \(R(S(v))\) has the form required in (12). More generally, if \(v\) ends in \(1\) and
\[
R(v)=V(1),\qquad V=(1,3)V_t,
\]
then the same boundary-gluing argument used for (15) gives
\[
R(S(v))=G\bigl(V(1),\overline{R^2(v)}\bigr).                   \tag{21}
\]
Since \(R(v)=(1,3)V_t(1)\), its first two unequal entries ensure that \(R^2(v)\) starts with \(1\) followed by some entry; it is nonempty beyond that first entry because the initial \(1,3\) already form two different runs. Consequently \(\overline{R^2(v)}\) ends in \(1\). Gluing at the middle in (21) does not affect the initial entries \((1,3)\) of \(V\), and it does not affect that final \(1\). This remains true in both cases \(V_t=\varnothing\) and \(V_t\neq\varnothing\); in the first case one glues directly after the displayed \((1,3)\), and in the second case the extra entries merely lie between the preserved prefix and suffix. Thus
\[
R(S(v))=V'(1)
\]
for some \(V'\) beginning with \((1,3)\). This completes the proof of the preservation assertion (13).

We now establish the initial good pair by a finite calculation. Iterating (4) gives
\[
W_3=(2,1,1,1,3,1)
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
W_7={}&(2,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,3,1,\\
&1,1,1,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,3,1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Their relevant run-length lists are
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(W_7)={}&(1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,1,1,7,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,1),\\
R^2(W_7)={}&(1,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,5,1,1,1,6),\\
R^3(W_7)={}&(6,1,1,1,3,1),\\
R(W_3)={}&(1,3,1,1).
\end{aligned}                                                   \tag{22}
\]
These equalities are obtained simply by grouping equal adjacent entries. They verify goodness with
\[
\begin{aligned}
C&=(1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,1,1,7,1,3,1,1,1,1,1),\\
D&=(1,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,5,1,1,1),\\
E&=(6,1,1,1,3),\\
V&=(1,3,1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, these have precisely the beginnings and endings in (10) and (12), both \(W_7\) and \(W_3\) begin with \((2,1,1,1,3)\) and end in \(1\), and
\[
R^3(W_7)=(6,1,1,1,3,1)=(6)\operatorname{tail}(W_3).
\]
By (13) and induction, therefore,
\[
(W_{k+7},W_{k+3})\text{ is good for every }k\geq0.             \tag{23}
\]

We extract from this invariant exactly the two length identities that will be needed. Apply (15) to \(x=W_{k+7}\). Since \(S(x)=W_{k+8}\), and since
\[
R(x)=C(1),\qquad R^2(x)=D(6),
\]
formula (15) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
|R(W_{k+8})|
 &=|C|+1+|D|,\\
|R(W_{k+7})|&=|C|+1,\\
|R^2(W_{k+7})|&=|D|+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
|R(W_{k+8})|+1
 =|R(W_{k+7})|+|R^2(W_{k+7})|.                                \tag{24}
\]
Similarly, (16) gives
\[
|R^2(W_{k+8})|=|D|+2+|E|.
\]
But (11) says
\[
E(1)=(6)\operatorname{tail}(W_{k+3}),
\]
so \(|E|+1=|W_{k+3}|\). Since \(|R^2(W_{k+7})|=|D|+1\), we obtain
\[
|R^2(W_{k+8})|
 =|R^2(W_{k+7})|+|W_{k+3}|.                                   \tag{25}
\]

We now package (7), (8), (24), and (25) into a fixed nonnegative recurrence. For \(k\geq0\), define the eight-component vector
\[
X_k=\bigl(
 a(k+10),
 |W_{k+7}|,
 |R(W_{k+7})|,
 |R^2(W_{k+7})|-1,
 |W_{k+6}|,
 |W_{k+5}|,
 |W_{k+4}|,
 |W_{k+3}|
\bigr).                                                        \tag{26}
\]
All entries are natural numbers. In particular, every \(W_j\) is nonempty by (4), and so its first and second run-length iterates are nonempty. Thus \(|R^2(W_j)|\geq1\), which justifies the fourth coordinate.

If \(F\) denotes the linear map
\[
F(x_0,\ldots,x_7)=
(x_0+x_1,\ x_1+x_2,\ x_2+x_3,\ x_3+x_7,\ x_1,\ x_4,\ x_5,\ x_6), \tag{27}
\]
then
\[
X_{k+1}=F(X_k).                                                 \tag{28}
\]
Indeed, the first coordinate is (7) with index \(k+7\); the second is (8); the third follows from (24):
\[
|R(W_{k+8})|
=|R(W_{k+7})|+\bigl(|R^2(W_{k+7})|-1\bigr);
\]
the fourth follows from (25):
\[
|R^2(W_{k+8})|-1
=\bigl(|R^2(W_{k+7})|-1\bigr)+|W_{k+3}|;
\]
and the last four coordinates are shifts.

We next prove two domination facts. First, every coordinate of \(X_k\) is at most its first coordinate:
\[
(X_k)_i\leq (X_k)_0\qquad(0\leq i\leq7).                      \tag{29}
\]
By (6),
\[
(X_k)_0=a(k+10)=\sum W_{k+7}.
\]
Every entry of every \(W_j\) is positive: this is true for \(W_0=(2)\), and (4) preserves it because run lengths are positive. Therefore
\[
|W_{k+7}|\leq\sum W_{k+7}.
\]
By (3),
\[
|R(W_{k+7})|\leq |W_{k+7}|,
\qquad
|R^2(W_{k+7})|-1\leq |W_{k+7}|.
\]
Finally, (8) shows that \(|W_j|\) is nondecreasing in \(j\), so each of \(|W_{k+6}|,\ldots,|W_{k+3}|\) is at most \(|W_{k+7}|\). This proves (29).

Second, every coordinate of \(X_0\) is at least \(1\):
\[
(X_0)_i\geq1.                                                  \tag{30}
\]
The coordinates involving \(W_3,\ldots,W_7\) and \(R(W_7)\) are positive because these lists are nonempty. The first coordinate is positive because it is the sum of the positive entries of \(W_7\). For the fourth coordinate we need \(|R^2(W_7)|\geq2\), and this is explicit in (22), where \(R^2(W_7)\) has thirteen entries. Thus (30) holds.

The map \(F\) has nonnegative integer coefficients and commutes with multiplication by a scalar. In particular, if two nonnegative vectors \(p,q\) satisfy
\[
p_i\leq c q_i\quad\text{for every }i,
\]
then inspection of the eight formulas in (27) gives
\[
F(p)_i\leq cF(q)_i\quad\text{for every }i.                    \tag{31}
\]

We claim that, for all \(m,n\geq0\) and every coordinate \(i\),
\[
(X_{m+n})_i\leq (X_m)_i\,(X_n)_0.                              \tag{32}
\]
For \(m=0\), (29) gives \((X_n)_i\leq(X_n)_0\), while (30) gives \((X_0)_i\geq1\), so
\[
(X_n)_i\leq (X_0)_i(X_n)_0.
\]
Suppose (32) holds for \(m\). Applying (31) with \(p=X_{m+n}\), \(q=X_m\), and \(c=(X_n)_0\), and then using (28), gives
\[
(X_{m+n+1})_i\leq (X_{m+1})_i(X_n)_0.
\]
Since \(m+n+1=(m+1)+n\), this is the induction step. Hence (32) is proved.

Let
\[
B_k=(X_k)_0=a(k+10).                                           \tag{33}
\]
Taking \(i=0\) in (32) yields the submultiplicative inequality
\[
B_{m+n}\leq B_mB_n                                             \tag{34}
\]
for all \(m,n\geq0\). Also \(B_n>0\), indeed \(B_n\geq1\).

We now use the standard subadditive argument. Define
\[
u_n=\log B_n.
\]
Since logarithm is increasing on the positive reals, (34) implies
\[
u_{m+n}\leq u_m+u_n.                                       \tag{35}
\]
Thus \((u_n)\) is subadditive. Moreover \(B_n\geq1\), so \(u_n\geq0\). Fekete's subadditive lemma therefore applies: the limit
\[
\lambda=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{u_n}{n}
       =\inf_{n\geq1}\frac{u_n}{n}                             \tag{36}
\]
exists as a finite real number. (A brief proof is as follows: for fixed \(q\), write \(n=kq+r\), \(0\leq r<q\); repeated use of (35) gives \(u_n\leq ku_q+u_r\), so \(\limsup u_n/n\leq u_q/q\). Taking the infimum over \(q\), while the reverse inequality follows from the definition of the infimum, proves convergence. Nonnegativity rules out \(-\infty\).)

Exponentiating (36), using continuity of the exponential function, gives
\[
B_n^{1/n}
 =\exp\!\left(\frac{\log B_n}{n}\right)
 \longrightarrow e^\lambda=:L.                               \tag{37}
\]

It remains to remove the shift by \(10\). For \(k\geq1\), (33) gives
\[
a(k+10)^{1/(k+10)}
 =\left(B_k^{1/k}\right)^{k/(k+10)}.                           \tag{38}
\]
By (37), the first base on the right tends to \(L=e^\lambda>0\), while
\[
\frac{k}{k+10}\longrightarrow1.
\]
Continuity of \((x,t)\mapsto x^t\) for \(x>0\) therefore shows from (38) that
\[
a(k+10)^{1/(k+10)}\longrightarrow L.
\]
Deleting or adding finitely many terms does not affect convergence of a sequence, so finally
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty}a(n)^{1/n}=L=e^\lambda}
\]
exists, where equivalently
\[
\lambda=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{\log a(k+10)}{k}
       =\inf_{k\geq1}\frac{\log a(k+10)}{k}.
\]
This proves the conjectured existence of the limit.
